say.text: A 19-year-old with suspected appendicitis describes the course of his pain over 12 hours.
Which course is typical?

choices.label: Right lower belly from the start, and it never moves
Starts at the navel, then moves to the right lower belly
Right lower belly from the start, then spreads to the navel
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Early pain comes from the gut wall, whose visceral nerves enter at T10. Which region does T10 cover?
Constant right-sided pain feels right, because the localised pain is the picture most people remember.
But early appendiceal pain comes from visceral fibres at T10, so it sits round the navel and only settles in the right iliac fossa later.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the start: the localised pain is the end of the story, not the first act.

say.text: Pain that starts on the right and climbs to the navel is tempting, because the right-sided pain is the one you remember.
But the course runs the other way: the navel comes first, and the pain moves down to the right iliac fossa.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace the course from the first hour, not from the clinic picture.

say.text: Yes. The pain starts periumbilical, from visceral afferents at T10.
It shifts to the right iliac fossa when the parietal peritoneum is involved.

choices.label: Skip the teaching, go to the blockage

say.text: Two regions, two nerve supplies. Visceral pain comes from the gut wall, enters at T10 and sits round the navel.
Somatic pain comes from the parietal peritoneum and is localised to the right iliac fossa.
Pain moves when the inflammation moves from the gut wall out to the peritoneum.
The pain localises to the right iliac fossa only after the early stage.
What causes that localisation?

choices.label: Rising lumen pressure stimulates T10 fibres more strongly
Wall ischaemia starts before the lumen is blocked
Inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, giving somatic pain
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Pain from the gut wall reaches you through T10 fibres. Which tissue, lining the abdominal wall, can point to a spot?
Pressure is the first real change inside the lumen, so it feels like the cause of where the pain sits.
But distension acts through the same T10 visceral fibres, which can only give periumbilical pain. Localisation needs the parietal peritoneum.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so localisation is the job of the peritoneum, not of the pressure.

say.text: Ischaemia is the dangerous event you remember, so it feels like it could come first.
But the blocked lumen raises pressure first, and the arterial compromise comes after. Ischaemia is late in the chain.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace the chain from the lumen outward, not back from the gangrene.

say.text: Follow the chain from the lumen: obstruction, continued mucus, rising pressure, venous congestion. Only then does the arterial supply fail.
The pain localises when inflammation reaches the peritoneum, not when the lumen first blocks.
Think of a blocked drain: the water backs up first, and the pipe gives way at its weakest point.
Yes. Inflammation reaching the parietal peritoneum makes the pain somatic and localised to the right iliac fossa.
The appendicular artery is a branch of the ileocolic artery, and it runs in the mesoappendix.
It is an end artery: once it thromboses, gangrene follows, usually first at the antimesenteric border.
So thrombosis of this one artery leads straight to gangrene and perforation.
The appendicular artery thromboses. Which outcome follows, and why so fast?

choices.label: Gangrene first, then the lumen blocks
Pressure rises only after the artery fails
Gangrene and perforation, since it is an end artery
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether another artery can back up the appendix when this one clots. The answer is in what kind of artery it is.
Gangrene is the outcome you remember most, so starting the story from it feels natural.
But gangrene is downstream: the lumen blocks, pressure rises, and only then does the artery fail.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trace the chain from the lumen, not from the end picture.

say.text: The artery is what a surgeon worries about, so its failure feels like the first event.
But raised pressure is the first step: the obstructed lumen compromises the arterial supply, not the other way round.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the arrow runs from the lumen to the artery, not back.

say.text: Yes. Because the appendicular artery is an end artery, its thrombosis gives gangrene and perforation with no backup.
Murphy's sequence describes the order of symptoms in typical appendicitis.
Which order is it?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with the first symptom the patient notices, then ask what the gut does after that.
Vomiting is the symptom many patients mention first, so it feels like the opening act.
But in appendicitis vomiting follows the pain; it comes after the pain has started.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the order is the clue: pain first, vomiting only after.

say.text: A fever feels like the sign of infection, so putting it first seems natural.
But fever is usually low-grade and comes last; a high fever points towards perforation or another diagnosis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fever is the late sign, not the opening one.

say.text: Yes. Pain first, then vomiting, then a low-grade fever.
Pain comes first, from the gut wall stretching. Anorexia is almost constant, and nausea with a few vomits follows the onset of pain.
Fever comes last and is usually low-grade.
So a story where vomiting came first argues against appendicitis, and a high fever points to perforation.
A young adult vomited several times through the morning, then developed diffuse abdominal pain and loose stools.
Which reading fits best?

choices.label: Gastroenteritis more likely, since vomiting came before the pain
Appendicitis, since vomiting is usually the first symptom
Appendicitis, since fever and vomiting come before the pain
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Find which symptom the story gives first, then ask which picture that order favours.
Yes. Vomiting before pain points away from appendicitis, where the pain comes first.
Vomiting is often the first symptom patients mention, so it feels like the opening act.
But in appendicitis the pain comes first and vomiting follows it. Vomiting before pain argues against this diagnosis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so use the order as a filter: pain first, vomiting later.

say.text: Fever with vomiting looks like an early systemic infection, so this reading is tempting.
But fever is usually low-grade and comes last, after the pain and vomiting. The order is the discriminator.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fever is the late sign, not the early one.

say.text: Two ways to block the lumen: a swollen lymphoid wall, or a hard faecolith sitting in the lumen.
A 9-year-old has had a viral illness, then right iliac fossa pain. Which block fits?

choices.label: The hard faecolith in the lumen
Either one; age makes no difference
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Lymphoid tissue is abundant in the young and shrinks with age. Which tissue is abundant in this 9-year-old's appendix?
A faecolith is the textbook block, so it is tempting whenever the question is about obstruction.
But a faecolith is the adult cause. In a child, lymphoid tissue is abundant and swells after a viral illness.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link the cause to the age: children have the lymphoid tissue to block the lumen.

say.text: Both can block a lumen, so calling them equal feels fair.
But the age changes which block is common: lymphoid hyperplasia in children and young people, a faecolith in adults.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so age is the cue before the cause.

say.text: In children the lymphoid tissue is maximal and swells after viral infection, so lymphoid hyperplasia blocks the lumen.
In adults the lymphoid tissue has atrophied, and a faecolith is the commonest block.
The age in the stem decides which block you are looking for.
Yes. A swollen lymphoid wall is the child's block, after viral infection.
The age in the stem decides the cause, so check it first.
